content: The Yuzpe Regimen is a method of emergency contraception that involves the use of a combination of estrogen and progestogen hormones. It must be initiated within 72 hours of unprotected sexual intercourse to be effective. However, this method has largely been replaced by progestogen-only hormonal regimens due to their improved efficacy and reduced side effects. The Yuzpe method was first developed by Canadian Professor A. Albert Yuzpe, who published studies in 1974 demonstrating its safety and effectiveness. This regimen works by allowing a woman who has had unprotected sex to prevent pregnancy through the administration of two doses of combined estrogen and progestogen hormones, taken 12 hours apart. The effectiveness of the regimen is highest when started as soon as possible after intercourse, and its efficacy significantly decreases if initiated more than 72 hours after the event. In contrast, emergency intrauterine device (IUD) insertion can be effective for up to five days after ovulation, which may extend beyond five days after the risky sexual encounter. The hormones in the Yuzpe Regimen are delivered via combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs). Depending on the brand of medication used, each dose may consist of 2 to 5 pills. For individuals taking medications that induce liver enzymes (e.g., rifamycin or certain anticonvulsants), which accelerate the breakdown of other drugs, a higher hormone dose may be required. In such cases, the insertion of an IUD may be a more suitable alternative. The standard Yuzpe Regimen involves taking two tablets, each containing 50 µg of ethinyl estradiol and 250 µg of levonorgestrel, followed by a second identical dose 12 hours later. It is important to note that this method does not guarantee the prevention of pregnancy. Additionally, the hormones may cause the subsequent menstrual period to occur a few days earlier or later than expected. If the period is delayed by more than three days, a pregnancy test should be performed. The Yuzpe Regimen does not provide protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Progestogen-only emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), which do not contain an estrogen component, have demonstrated greater efficacy and fewer side effects compared to the Yuzpe method. A single dose of 100 mg mifepristone is also more effective than the Yuzpe Regimen. Temporary but generally minor side effects of the Yuzpe Regimen include nausea, vomiting, breast tenderness, irregular bleeding, headache, and dizziness. If vomiting occurs within three hours of taking a dose, the hormones may not have been adequately absorbed, and an additional dose should be taken. To minimize nausea or vomiting, the following measures may be helpful: Take the pills with food. If particularly sensitive to nausea, consider taking an antiemetic such as Dramamine or Bonine one hour before the pills (though this is not mandatory). Schedule the second dose to be taken before bedtime. Many commonly available combined oral contraceptive pills can be used for the Yuzpe Regimen, even if they are not specifically labeled for this purpose. Off-label use of approved medications is both legal and common in American medical practice. In February 1997, the FDA declared the emergency contraceptive use of certain birth control pills, following the Yuzpe Regimen, to be safe and effective. However, dedicated Yuzpe Regimen products, such as Preven in the U.S. and Schering-PC4 in the U.K., were discontinued after the introduction of progestogen-only ECPs, such as Plan B in the U.S. and Levonelle in the U.K.
